content: Vilanterol (VI) is a long-acting beta2-agonist (LABA) that works by binding to beta2-adrenoceptors on airway smooth muscle, leading to bronchodilation. LABA therapy is a well-established treatment for asthma in adults, as outlined in the British Thoracic Society (BTS) Guidelines for the Management of Asthma. This therapy improves symptoms, enhances lung function, and reduces the frequency of exacerbations. Currently, the most commonly used LABAs for asthma management, such as formoterol and salmeterol, require administration twice daily. In contrast, VI offers the advantage of once-daily dosing. Fluticasone furoate (FF) is an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) that is also recommended by the BTS asthma guidelines. ICS therapy is a cornerstone of asthma management, as it reduces airway inflammation and hyper-responsiveness. Regular use of ICS improves both symptoms and lung function. ICSs are typically prescribed as preventer medications for patients who use reliever medications, such as short-acting beta2-agonists (SABAs) like salbutamol, three or more times per week. Most ICS treatments require twice-daily administration, although two once-daily ICS options, ciclesonide and mometasone, are currently available. At present, only one once-daily ICS/LABA combination, FF/VI, is available, while other combination inhalers require twice-daily administration. The objective of this review was to compare the effects of VI and FF in combination versus placebo or other ICSs and/or LABAs on acute exacerbations and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in adults and children with chronic asthma. To achieve this, the authors searched the Cochrane Airways Group Register of trials, clinical trial registries, manufacturers' websites, and reference lists of included studies up to June 2016. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving adults and children diagnosed with asthma. These studies compared the combination of VI and FF with placebo or other ICSs and/or LABAs. The primary outcomes assessed were health-related quality of life, severe asthma exacerbations (defined as hospital admissions or the need for oral corticosteroids), and serious adverse events. Data were independently extracted and analyzed by two review authors using a fixed-effect model and standard Cochrane methods. A total of 14 studies met the inclusion criteria, involving 6641 randomized participants, of whom 5638 completed the studies. The studies ranged in duration from two to 78 weeks and were generally of good methodological quality. The review included 10 comparisons for the 100/25 mcg dose of VI/FF and three comparisons for the 200/25 mcg dose. The 100/25 mcg dose was compared with placebo, the same dose of FF or VI alone, fluticasone propionate (FP) 500 mcg twice daily, and fluticasone propionate/salmeterol (FP/SAL) in various doses. The 200/25 mcg dose was compared with placebo, FP 500 mcg, and the same dose of FF alone. The review found limited opportunities to combine results from the 14 studies in meta-analyses. Data for the pre-specified primary outcomes were tabulated. There was insufficient information to determine whether once-daily VI/FF was superior or inferior to twice-daily FP/SAL in terms of efficacy or safety. Only one study assessed health-related quality of life when comparing VI/FF 100/25 mcg with placebo, showing a significant advantage for VI/FF 100/25 mcg (mean difference 0.30, 95% confidence interval 0.14 to 0.46; 329 participants). This was considered moderate-quality evidence. Two studies compared VI/FF 100/25 mcg with placebo for exacerbations, but neither reported any exacerbations in either treatment arm. Five studies assessed serious adverse events for VI/FF 100/25 mcg versus placebo, and none reported any serious adverse events in either group. No relevant comparisons were available for the higher dose of VI/FF (200/25 mcg) versus placebo. The small number of studies contributing to each comparison limited the ability to draw robust conclusions for clinical practice. Additionally, the studies were not of sufficient duration to assess long-term side effects. The authors concluded that some evidence suggests clear benefits of the VI/FF combination compared with placebo, particularly in terms of forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) and peak expiratory flow. However, the variety of questions addressed in the included studies prevented the authors from drawing firm conclusions. There was insufficient information to determine whether once-daily VI/FF is better or worse than twice-daily FP/SAL in terms of efficacy or safety. More research is needed to address the uncertainties identified in this review. Replication of these findings in future studies is necessary to draw more robust conclusions. Only five of the 14 included studies provided data on health-related quality of life, and only six recorded asthma exacerbations. Furthermore, only one study focused on pediatric patients, making it impossible to draw conclusions for this population. Additional research is required, particularly in the primary outcome areas, to enable firmer conclusions in future updates of this review.
